Arianna Polonio Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email ARIANNA POLONIO/MORRISON COUNTY RECORD Kowalczuks family is based in Brainerd, MN. They own a Polish food truck and travel with a 60 mile radius to share Iwona’s cooking around central Minnesota. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Iwona’s Pierogies not only pays tribute to the Polish roots of the Kowalczuks family, but also serves as an opportunity to feed the significant Polish community of Brainerd and Little Falls. Lukasz Kowalczuk is the son of Iwona and Walmar Kowalczuk, and a first-generation Polish-American. Walmar comes from a small town next to Warsaw and Iwona from the town of Suwalki, they met in the U.S. while working. They lived in Grand Junction, Colorado and ran a family hotel for 22 years before moving to Central Minnesota in 2004. Lukasz shared that after he graduated college, his family moved to Central Minnesota looking for larger lakes since he and his dad are big fishermen. They first settled in the 37 Acre RV and Campground where they encountered a large community of third and fourth generations of polish. “We realized how many Polish folks are around in this area and there was no one offering Polish food,” Lucasz said. It was then that the Kowalczuk’s realized there could be a demand for Polish food. They eventually settled in Brainerd and originally looked at brick and mortar spaces, but after spending winter in Brainerd, they noticed few people were keen on going outside. “It’s kind of a ghost town during the winter. We told ourselves, ‘you know what, we have to be mobile if we want to be successful.’ That’s how we decided on a food truck,” Lukasz said. The food truck also enhances the chances to achieve more customers from out of town. “In the summertime, every town gets pretty booked up,” Lukasz said. “We don’t tend to travel further than a 60-mile radius of Brainerd, but it gives the opportunity to people who haven’t tried Polish food, or just want to get a reminder of their grandmother’s cooking. It gives a lot more opportunities to people.” Some of the towns they travel to include Little Falls, Walker, St. Cloud, Crosby and Cross Lake. “We want to share the culture of what I’ve experienced, what I grew up [with], and share my mother’s wonderful cooking to everyone out there.” Lucasz said. Their most popular dish is the pierogies, followed by the golabki cabbage rolls. “We offer caramelized onions and bacon on top of the pierogies and that’s something that we just offer to everyone. It’s no additional charge, we want to offer the most traditional pierogies.” Lukasz said. The pierogies are filled with pork, chicken or beef. They also offer a potato and cheese pierogi with white farmer’s cheese. The American favorite is the potato bacon cheddar pierogi, while not a polish traditional dish, it is still enjoyed by many. Their menu also includes kielbasa (Polish sausages), which is Lukasz’s favorite. The biggest highlight of Iwona’s Pierogies is having polish immigrants and descendants enjoying the food that reminds them of their hometown and family. Lukasz says that about 60% of their customers are third or fourth-generation Polish. “A lot of people tell me, it reminds them of their grandmother’s cooking, and they’re really excited that our truck is there, and gives them the opportunity to remind them of their childhood,” Lukasz said. “I do have a handful of customers that come up to the truck and speak fluent Polish, which is quite nice. They are really grateful to see a Polish truck and have Polish people in their community as well.” The Kowalczuks work hard most of the year, working six days a week. During the winter time they reduce their work days. Finally, what the Kowalczuks enjoy the most about owning a food truck is being able to spend family time together. To tell customers where Iwona’s Pierogies is heading next, the family posts their location schedule on their business’ Facebook page under the same name — Iwona’s Pierogies. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP View image in fullscreen The AfD’s candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, says ‘we have written history’ and the party has a clear mandate to govern. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP Germany Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority Alternative für Deutschland surges to victory in Saxony-Anhalt as Friedrich Merz’s CDU slumps to disastrous result AfD thanks Elon Musk as France warns state election win a ‘serious moment’ Kate Connolly in Berlin Sun 6 Sep 2026 22.42 EDT First published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war. The party of Germany’s unpopular chancellor Friedrich Merz, the Christian Democrats (CDU), slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. AfD’s candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said “we have written history” and the party had a clear mandate to govern. He told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that “things cannot carry on like this”. “A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz,” Siegmund said. Germany’s far-right AfD thanks Elon Musk as France warns state election win a ‘serious moment’ Read more AfD was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the party. AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund, 35, said it would not engage in “games” such as a minority government. But it was not evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it. AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin. That was far ahead of Merz’s CDU , which polled 17.2% – losing about half its support – and won 15 seats. The centre-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece. The BSW party, which has said it would not elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticises the “firewall” against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats. Participation in the election was at a record high of 76.5%. Addressing jubilant supporters after ⁠exit polls had been published, Siegmund said his party was ready to ⁠reach out ​to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change. “We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue ​better policies,” he said, adding that themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate. The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out. Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era. She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how AfD could rule. About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state. Final polls had shown AfD to have about 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties. View image in fullscreen Siegmund celebrating with AfD’s co-leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right) after polls closed on Sunday. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033. If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools. Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ ostalgie ”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status. Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”. Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”. On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.” The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said. The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers. Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased. Photograph: Ferdi Limani/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Thaçi faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity including murder, torture and persecution. Photograph: Ferdi Limani/Getty Images War crimes Kosovo’s former president jailed for 25 years over war crimes Hashim Thaçi, 58, was convicted by The Hague for crimes committed while he was senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.40 EDT First published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders, committed during his time as a senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army during the country’s war for independence from Serbia in the late 1990s. The European-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers, convicted Thaci, 58, and three other former senior commanders of 96 murders, and counts of torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention directed at political opponents and civilians. The convictions come at the end of a years-long process, strongly opposed by many in Kosovo , to bring accountability for crimes committed by KLA commanders during the 1998-99 war in which war crimes were committed by both sides. Thaçi, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face charges, stood in silence in The Hague as the presiding judge Charles Smith read out the sentence. The former president, who served as the head of political directorate of the KLA’s general staff, faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity alongside the three other former leaders of the KLA who are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland. In addition to the murders, Thaçi was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50. View image in fullscreen Crowds chant as people wait for the decision of The Kosovo Specialist Chambers against leaders of former Kosovo Liberation Army. Photograph: Ferdi Limani/Getty Images Once a hardliner, Thaçi shifted towards a more moderate political identity after being courted by western diplomats who suggested he could be a central figure in Kosovo’s post-war settlement. At the heart of the prosecution’s case was the degree to which the convicted men had senior operational command over the KLA as a centrally-led armed force and whether the crimes amounted to a pattern of abuse. The ⁠court ruled that Thaçi had “actively participated in and encouraged crimes”. Smith said: “The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious”. He added: “The so-called ​intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and ‌killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based ‌on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated.” Smith said Thaçi “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage crimes but insisted the trial was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army” or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia. Thaçi could appeal the verdict. Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaçi and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi who had all denied the charges against them. Krasniqi received 25 years in prison, Selimi 13 years and Veseli 18 years. Thaçi also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin this month. The three-judge panel ⁠dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity and said prosecutors had failed to show these happened as part ​of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population ​as a whole. Known by the nom de guerre of Commander Snake during the war, Thaçi stood out among the KLA leadership as an intelligent and articulate figure who would later charm diplomats – most notably the US secretary of state Madeleine Albright – at the negotiations in Rambouillet that ended the conflict. But behind the self-assured image he projected as a senior political figure, he was long dogged by allegations of a darker and more ruthless side from his time as a wartime commander. Thaçi’s defence partly rested on the notion that while serious abuses did occur, the KLA was a not a strictly centralised organisation, claiming that Thaçi’s senior position in the rebel group did not indicate culpability for crimes committed by local units. “Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaçi told judges in February. The trial was opposed by many in Kosovo. Outside the court, Kosovo foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, told the media: “A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision,.” Thaçi’s PDK party called the verdict “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army”. In Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence. Some started shouting “UCK,” the Albanian-language acronym for the KLA. Thaçi, who was born in Kosovo’s rugged Drenica mountains – the KLA heartland – was a philosophy student who rose through the KLA’s ranks, returning from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence. Thaçi served in a series of senior political roles after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the The Hague. After the war, Thaçi became a central political figure and was instrumental in Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence. Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of Nato airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/sua/.text: Vladimir Putin și Donald Trump ar urma să continue discuțiile privind încheierea războiului din Ucraina la summitul APEC, programat săptămâna viitoare în China, a anunțat consilierul liderului de la Kremlin, Iuri Ușakov. Întâlnirea ar urma să aibă loc în contextul unui posibil summit trilateral cu Xi Jinping, în timp ce Ucraina și liderii europeni insistă că nu pot fi excluși din negocierile care le privesc securitatea și viitorul, potrivit Kyiv Post . Summitul APEC va avea loc în orașul Shenzhen, din sudul Chinei, în perioada 18-19 noiembrie. Discuțiile dintre Putin și Trump ar urma să se desfășoare în contextul unei întâlniri trilaterale planificate cu președintele chinez Xi Jinping, pe care Ușakov a descris-o drept prima reuniune într-un asemenea format. „Desigur, în cadrul întâlnirii planificate cu acesta la summitul APEC de la Shenzhen, vor continua discuțiile privind întreaga gamă de probleme legate de soluționarea conflictului”, a declarat Ușakov, potrivit agenției RIA Novosti. Anunțul vine după întâlnirea de aproximativ două ore și jumătate pe care Putin a avut-o la Kremlin cu reprezentanții americani Steve Witkoff și Jared Kushner. Cei doi au ajuns la Moscova după încheierea discuțiilor trilaterale de două zile desfășurate la Abu Dhabi, în perioada 10-11 noiembrie. Potrivit unui alt raport al agenției Interfax-Ru, Kremlinul va menține legătura cu Witkoff și Kushner și va analiza împreună cu emisarii americani evoluțiile negocierilor înaintea unei eventuale întâlniri între Putin și Trump în China. La momentul publicării informației, Casa Albă nu confirmase participarea lui Donald Trump la summit. Ideea unei întâlniri trilaterale între liderii Statelor Unite, Rusiei și Chinei ar fi fost lansată de Vladimir Putin în timpul unei convorbiri telefonice cu Donald Trump, pe 9 octombrie, potrivit unui fost oficial al serviciilor de informații ruse citat de The Wall Street Journal pe 19 octombrie. Sursa a susținut că liderul de la Kremlin vedea această reuniune ca pe o ocazie de a organiza o nouă conferință în stilul celei de la Yalta și de a împărți lumea în sfere de influență. În timpul aceleiași convorbiri telefonice, cei doi lideri ar fi ajuns la un acord privind motorina, ceea ce a fost urmat de câteva săptămâni de tensiuni tot mai mari între Washington și Kiev. Un oficial american de rang înalt a confirmat că Putin a făcut propunerea unei întâlniri trilaterale. Separat, secretarul de stat american Marco Rubio a declarat că existau discuții privind o posibilă reuniune între Trump, Putin și Xi Jinping, în vederea negocierii încheierii războiului declanșat de Rusia împotriva Ucrainei. Într-un interviu acordat postului public rus Vesti, pe 25 octombrie, Iuri Ușakov a confirmat că pregătirile pentru un summit trilateral începuseră deja. China a recunoscut abia la începutul lunii noiembrie că se află în contact cu Washingtonul și Moscova în legătură cu o posibilă reuniune. Beijingul nu a oferit însă detalii despre formatul sau agenda acesteia. Posibilitatea unei întâlniri între Trump, Putin și Xi Jinping a provocat reacții atât la Kiev, cât și în capitalele europene. Ucraina și partenerii săi europeni au insistat că trebuie să participe la orice discuții care privesc viitorul țării și arhitectura sa de securitate. Președintele ucrainean Volodimir Zelenski a respins ideea ca deciziile privind Ucraina să fie luate fără participarea Kievului. La rândul său, ministrul de externe Andrii Sîbiha a avertizat că un asemenea summit riscă să-l încurajeze pe Vladimir Putin să continue războiul, în loc să contribuie la încheierea lui. Liderii europeni au transmis, de asemenea, că niciun acord privind Ucraina nu poate fi impus acestei țări sau Europei fără consimțământul lor. Cu toate acestea, reprezentanții europeni au fost ținuți în afara negocierilor principale de la Abu Dhabi. Marea Britanie, Franța, Germania, Italia, NATO și Comisia Europeană au purtat consultări separate cu oficialii de la Kiev și Washington. În acest context, ministrul rus de externe Serghei Lavrov le-ar fi transmis oficialilor europeni să „rămână la hotel”. Totuși, emisarul american Steve Witkoff a sugerat că europenii ar putea fi implicați în următoarea rundă de discuții. „Sperăm că vom putea anunța în curând, poate chiar la sfârșitul acestei reuniuni, următoarea întâlnire trilaterală la care vor participa și europenii”, a declarat el, potrivit CNN.
